@DaddyBenson  Remember 6700 to 6900 has bigger bus speeds and bandwidth to push more data.
The 6600 has to make up for it in higher clock speeds due to smaller bus and bandwidth.

This mean the real test is from I/O related benchmarks, pushing data into VRAM and maxing it out.

Most games doesn't push that much data unless it uses AI and complex computing that requires a lot of math and simulations...
A real test is running simulators like racing and such?

Granted raytracing is complex math as well but it utilizes required cores to do so, it also isn't AI related for game component use cases...

So if a game had no graphical RT, but has AI based learning and gameplay involving elements using Physics based RT, then it would see far better usage of it.

Like the enemy sees a reflection of you hiding behind cover, without the whole graphical reflection part on your screen.

The extra power consumption and price is not worth it. From my early testing undervolting the card is the best option to raise performance a bit (it will clock higher within the power limit):
Super Position 3440x1400 High:
5700 XT @ 975mv 1900T ~1850MHz effective= 5824
6800 XT @ Stock 2408T~ 2210MHz effective = 11710
6800 XT @ 1000mvT 2408T ~2350MHz effective = 12091
6800 XT @ 1000mvT 2500T ~2400MHz effective = 12383

With slight UV you get Nitro+ performance at Reference power. with the 2500T you have a slightly higher performance. Lowering the voltage even more will net a slight boost but not all chips will be able to hit 2400MHz at 950-975mv.

They weren't any worse than anyone else, nor can I remember them being touted as being better, but back then the graphics chips didn't even need a heat sink, so cooling wasn't an issue. As this was a analogue signal the quality of the DAC could make the image displayed on the monitor look soft and it also limited the usable refresh rates and could limit the resolution. But other than that there wasn't much the graphics cards manufacturers could do but compete with price.
